title: Lesson 77: Capacity Planning and Performance at Scale: Headroom, Forecasting, and the Load You Cannot See
description: Capacity is not a server size. It is the amount of work your org can absorb before one specific constraint breaks, and how many months of growth you have left before it does.

questions.question: An org has a daily API allocation of 500,000 calls. Peak-day consumption is 325,000 and has grown 10 percent per quarter. Using the lesson's runway formula, which statement is correct?
options: Headroom is 35 percent, and runway is about 4.6 quarters, so roughly fourteen months.
Headroom is 35 percent, and runway is about 9 quarters, because growth of 10 percent per quarter takes 90 percent of the remaining time to reach the limit.
Headroom is 65 percent, and runway is about 2 quarters because the peak is already close to the limit.
Headroom is 35 percent, and runway cannot be computed without knowing the average consumption over the same period.
questions.explanation: Headroom is (500,000 - 325,000) / 500,000 = 35 percent. Runway is ln(500,000 / 325,000) / ln(1.10) = 0.4318 / 0.0953 = about 4.5 quarters, roughly fourteen months. The lesson shows this same calculation at 280,000 and 196,000.

questions.question: The service console's default list view filters a 12 million row Case object on Status != 'Closed', and it has slowed from two seconds to twenty. A stakeholder asks for more CPU capacity. What does the lesson say to do first?
options: Buy more capacity, because a scan on 12 million rows is a platform limit and cannot be fixed by design.

Fix the design first: the negation filter on a low-cardinality field causes a scan, so filter on a selective indexed value such as an IsClosed boolean, add a custom index, and decompose the query if multiple WHERE filters block index use.
Move the list view to a scheduled report, because list views are not indexable.
Convert the object to a Big Object so performance stays consistent at any volume.
questions.explanation: The lesson's decision rule puts the waste question first. The tuning guidance it cites says null and non-selective filters do not use the index, and in some cases multiple WHERE filters prevent index use, in which case you decompose into narrower queries. Buying capacity does not make a full-table scan faster.

questions.question: A monthly load of 400,000 records runs as one REST call per record against an allocation of 280,000 calls per day, and a developer says the sandbox test finished in 40 minutes so it is fine. What is the correct reading?
options: The test proves capacity is sufficient, because 40 minutes is well inside the nightly window.

The load alone exceeds the daily allocation at 400,000 calls, so callers fail and retries make it worse. It should move to Bulk API 2.0, whose batches draw from a separate allocation pool, and the sandbox result only proved data volume behavior, not production concurrency.
The load is acceptable because REST calls are not counted against the API allocation when they run outside business hours.
The load is acceptable if the developer raises the batch size in the REST request payload.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the cost unit is the call, not the record, so 400,000 records as individual REST calls consumes 400,000 calls against a 280,000 daily allocation. It also states that a full copy sandbox proves data-volume behavior and not concurrency, so a comfortable sandbox timing is a floor rather than a prediction.
